newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Crude Outlook - WTI seen lifted by expiry.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Crude Outlook - WTI seen lifted by expiry.

text.p: U.S. crude oil prices are likely to head higher this week, driven by short-covering ahead of the expiry of May futures, a brighter outlook for fundamentals and the recent uptick in distillate prices, market analysts said on Monday.

The May crude contract on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) was trading around $20.25-35 a barrel mid-morning, up some 40 cents from Friday's settlement. The contract expires on Tuesday, followed by the pipeline scheduling deadline in the cash market later in the week.
"We've seen some indications of a squeeze on May," said John Saucer, an analyst with investment bank Smith Barney in Houston. "There's a fair amount of shorts in this market."
As May activity winds down, traders are abuzz over signs that ARCO might deliver Bonny Light crude into NYMEX.

Exchange for Physical (EFPs) agreements have been commanding a premium of six to 12 cents a barrel over the past few weeks as traders rush to escape paper positions which might leave them with a crude grade other than the benchmark West Texas Intermediate/Cushing.
ARCO was heard to have already moved two to three million barrels of the Nigerian crude into Cushing in anticipation of a delivery. Company officials declined to comment.

Aside from the expiry, crude prices are getting a lift out of improved global fundamentals. U.S. Gulf Coast refiners are gearing up for gasoline season, European downstream margins have brightened and Asian refiners are shopping for crude again after coming out of turnarounds, analysts said.
"The fundamentals are not as bearish as everyone was talking about," said Tom Bentz of ING Derivatives in New York. "The demand for crude is there."
Also propping up crude prices are strong distillate prices.

"Distillates have been doing remarkably well in New York Harbor," Saucer said. Heating oil prices in New York Harbor are running four cents abover the May NYMEX contract, up from a three-cent premium about a week ago.
The uptick, which is unusual for springtime, is attributed to chilly weather and major suppliers' consequent shopping spree.
A spate of bullish news out of the Middle East has sharpened crude's upward shift.
On Monday, Iraq said it was sending helicopters to pick up returning Moslem pilgrims from the Saudi border despite a ban by the United States and other Western powers on Iraqi flights in the area.
The market was jittery over the flights' possible impact on the ongoing oil-for-food deal run by the United Nations.
Next door in Iran, local students marched on the German embassy to protest a Berlin court verdict accusing Tehran of ordering political killings.

Meanwhile, OPEC is trying to flex its muscle in the market in a bid to prop up prices. OPEC's president Libyan Oil Minister Abdalla el-Badri has called on OPEC members to restrain output, although it is not clear whether members have responded to the request, OPEC secretary General Rilwanu Lukman said on Monday.
The news was more "words not deeds," said Saucer. "But the market was already rising and that certainly didn't hurt."
